## Problem 1

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)

data("ny_noaa")

# Check data shape and structure
dim(ny_noaa)
glimpse(ny_noaa)
```

```{r}
# Check NA proportion of each variable
ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ mean(is.na(.))
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "proportion_missing"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(proportion_missing))
```

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains 2,595,176 observations and 7 variables. Each row represents a daily weather observation from a NOAA weather station in New York State. Key variables include station ID (`id`), date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`). The `date` variable is stored as a date, while `prcp`, `snow`, and `snwd` are stored as integers; `tmax` and `tmin` are currently stored as character variables and will require cleaning before analysis.

Missing data are a substantial issue in this dataset. Approximately 43.7% of observations are missing for both `tmin` and `tmax`, while 22.8% are missing for `snwd`, 14.7% for `snow`, and 5.6% for `prcp`. The station ID and date variables have no missing values.

```{r}
# Clean the NY NOAA data and create separate date variables
ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    # Extract year, month, and day from the date variable
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),

    # Convert temperature variables to degrees Celsius
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,

    # Convert precipitation, snowfall, and snow depth to millimeters
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    snow = snow / 10,
    snwd = snwd / 10
  )

# Check the structure of the cleaned dataset
glimpse(ny_noaa_clean)
```

I first cleaned the dataset by separating the date into year, month, and day variables and converting the weather measurements into more interpretable units.

```{r}
# Summarize the cleaned weather variables
ny_noaa_clean |>
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp, snow, snwd) |>
  summary()
```

```{r}
# Identify the most commonly observed snowfall values
ny_noaa_clean |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, with 2,008,508 observations. This is expected because snowfall occurs only on a relatively small number of days, so zero snowfall is much more common than any positive amount. Among nonzero values, small snowfall amounts such as 2.5 mm, 1.3 mm, and 5.1 mm are observed relatively frequently, which is consistent with light snowfall events being more common than heavy snowfall.

```{r}
# Calculate average maximum temperature in January and July

jan_jul_temp =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax))

# Label the month
jan_jul_temp =
  jan_jul_temp |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

# Plot average maximum temperature by station across years
ggplot(
  jan_jul_temp,
  aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15) +
  facet_wrap(~ month, ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Average January and July Maximum Temperatures by Station",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
Average maximum temperatures are substantially lower and more variable in January than in July. January station-level averages are generally centered near 0°C, while July averages are mostly in the mid-to-upper 20s °C. There is substantial year-to-year variation, especially in January, but no strong monotonic temporal trend is immediately apparent. A few unusually low station-year averages appear in both months and may represent outliers or stations with unusual local conditions.

```{r}
# Plot the joint distribution of maximum and minimum temperatures
temp_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax),
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 40) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "blue1",
    high = "blue4"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
# Keep positive snowfall values below 100 mm and summarize snowfall distributions within each year
snow_plot_data =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(
    snow > 0,
    snow < 100
  ) |>
  mutate(
    snow_bin = floor(snow / 5) * 5
  ) |>
  count(year, snow_bin) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  mutate(
    proportion = n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Plot snowfall distributions separately by year
snow_plot =
  snow_plot_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = snow_bin,
      y = factor(year),
      fill = proportion
    )
  ) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "skyblue1",
    high = "skyblue4"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm; 5-mm bins)",
    y = "Year",
    fill = "Within-year proportion"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=15}
# Create two-panel plot
library(patchwork)
temp_plot / snow_plot
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship, with most observations concentrated along an upward-sloping band. Most daily maximum temperatures are higher than the corresponding minimum temperatures, as expected. A small number of extreme observations appear far from the main distribution and may reflect unusual or erroneous measurements.

Across years, positive snowfall amounts below 100 mm are concentrated in the smaller snowfall bins, while larger snowfall amounts occur much less frequently. This pattern is fairly consistent across years, although some year-to-year variation is present.


## Problem 2

```{r, message=FALSE}
# Load demographic data
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  )

# Load accelerometer data
nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
```

```{r}
# Check dimensions and variable structure
dim(nhanes_covar)
glimpse(nhanes_covar)

# Check accelerometer dimensions and selected variables
dim(nhanes_accel)

nhanes_accel |>
  select(SEQN, min1:min5, min1436:min1440) |>
  glimpse()
```

```{r}
# Tidy accelerometer data into long format
nhanes_accel_tidy =
  nhanes_accel |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min"))
  )
```

```{r}
# Clean demographic variables
nhanes_covar_clean =
  nhanes_covar |>
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    complete.cases(sex, age, BMI, education)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )
```

```{r}
# Merge demographic and accelerometer data
nhanes_data =
  nhanes_accel_tidy |>
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar_clean,
    by = "SEQN"
  )
```

```{r}
# Check the cleaned and merged data
dim(nhanes_covar_clean)

nhanes_data |>
  select(SEQN, minute, MIMS, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
dim(nhanes_data)
```

```{r}
n_distinct(nhanes_data$SEQN)
```

After excluding participants younger than 21 years and those with missing demographic information, 228 participants remained. The accelerometer data were converted to long format with one observation per participant-minute, resulting in 328,320 observations.
